auxiliary_material: The study provides supporting context about antibiotic exposure timing windows (most commonly 30–60 days prior to ICI initiation), tumor types analyzed (NSCLC most frequently represented, plus RCC, UC, melanoma, HCC, CRC, gastric cancer), and treatment contexts (ICI monotherapy vs. combination with chemotherapy). The authors discuss mechanistic pathways linking ABT-induced gut dysbiosis to impaired ICI efficacy through depletion of beneficial commensal taxa (Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium) and reduced microbial metabolites affecting CD8+ T-cell responses. They also introduce the concept of microbial compartmentalization (gut versus intratumoral bacteria), citing Riaz et al. to illustrate context-dependent microbiome effects. The review notes that ABT effects persisted in ICI plus chemotherapy subgroup analysis (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.08–1.16 for OS). Quality assessment used MINORS and NOS scales, with included studies rated moderate to high quality.
outline_action: Use this systematic review's explicit limitation statement to document that class-specific antibiotic evidence is currently unavailable in ICI-treated populations. Cite the HR 1.16 for OS as the best available evidence for broad-spectrum ABT effects. Note that future prospective studies should incorporate granular and standardized antibiotic exposure metrics (including dose, duration, class, and timing relative to ICI initiation) as recommended by the authors. The mechanistic discussion about gut dysbiosis and specific commensal taxa can support rationale for why class-specific effects might exist but remain unproven. The microbial compartmentalization concept (gut vs. intratumoral) should be included when discussing mechanism complexity and context-dependency of microbiome-ICI interactions.
remaining_gap: While this systematic review confirms that current evidence supports only broad-spectrum ABT effects without class-specific differentiation, it does not identify any primary studies that perform head-to-head comparisons between specific antibiotic classes with reported hazard ratios and statistical significance. The review's limitation statement reflects the state of the primary literature rather than identifying specific comparative studies. No prospective comparative studies between antibiotic classes were identified in this review's search.
useful_material: This systematic review and meta-analysis explicitly addresses the gap by stating that class-specific antibiotic comparisons could not be performed due to heterogeneity in ABT definitions, exposure windows, and limited reporting of ABT classes across the 15 included studies (52,489 patients). The authors report: 'heterogeneity in ABT definitions, exposure windows, and reporting of ABT classes limited our ability to perform detailed class-specific or dose-dependent analyses.' Table 3 shows that many studies did not report specific antibiotic classes (marked 'NR'). The meta-analysis compared ABT exposure versus no ABT exposure only, finding ABT associated with worse OS (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.03–1.29) and a trend toward worse PFS (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.95–1.27). When antibiotic classes were reported, exposure predominantly involved broad-spectrum agents (beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, etc.) without head-to-head comparisons between classes. This satisfies the second success criterion: a clear statement from a systematic review that existing evidence only supports broad-spectrum antibiotic overall effects without class-specific differentiation.
